seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 91 HTS Chapter 18 lines: cocoa beans, cocoa paste, cocoa butter, cocoa powder and chocolate. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, the chocolate and sweetened-cocoa quotas, and the 2026 Section 301 duties by country (cocoa beans, butter and powder are exempt).

overview.intro:
Chapter 18 covers cocoa from bean to bar: cocoa beans (1801), shells (1802), cocoa paste or liquor (1803), cocoa butter (1804), unsweetened cocoa powder (1805) and chocolate and other food preparations containing cocoa (1806). It has **91 tariff lines**, and the duty depends almost entirely on which side of that split a product falls.

**Cocoa ingredients enter free or nearly free.** Beans, shells, butter and natural cocoa paste are Free; defatted paste is 0.2¢/kg and unsweetened powder 0.52¢/kg. Lines 1801–1805 are on the exemption lists of the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)) and the Brazil tariff, so no country pays an extra duty on them except China (7.5%, List 4A). They were $7.46B of the $13.32B the U.S. imported in 2025, mostly from Côte d'Ivoire, Ecuador, Ghana, Indonesia and Malaysia.

**Chocolate (1806) is where the duty is.** Retail bars and candy pay 5.6% or 6%. Bulk chocolate, chocolate crumb and sweetened cocoa powder sit under tariff-rate quotas: inside the quota they pay 3.5%–10% or Free, above it up to 52.8¢/kg + 8.5%. Since **July 24, 2026** chocolate from 60 economies also pays a Section 301 duty: 10% in total for the EU, 12.5% in total for Switzerland, +10% or +12.5% for most others, +20% for China and +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying chocolate from Canada and Mexico, which shipped $3.76B of it in 2025, pays no Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Cocoa beans, whole or broken, raw or roasted
productGroups.blurb: Raw or roasted cocoa beans, whole or broken (cocoa nibs are broken beans). Free for every country, and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties. The largest product in the chapter: $2.82B in 2025.

productGroups.label: Cocoa shells, husks, skins and other cocoa waste
productGroups.blurb: Cocoa shells, husks, skins and other cocoa waste. Free, and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. A very small trade.

productGroups.label: Cocoa paste, whether or not defatted
productGroups.blurb: Cocoa paste (cocoa mass or chocolate liquor). Natural paste is Free; defatted paste is 0.2¢/kg, Free with most FTAs and AGOA. Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties.

productGroups.label: Cocoa butter, fat and oil
productGroups.blurb: Cocoa butter, fat and oil. Free for every country and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties; most comes from Indonesia and Malaysia.

productGroups.label: Cocoa powder, not containing added sugar or other…
productGroups.blurb: Cocoa powder without added sugar or sweetener: 0.52¢/kg, Free under most FTAs and AGOA. Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. Sweetened cocoa powder is in 1806.10.

productGroups.label: Chocolate and other food preparations containing cocoa
productGroups.blurb: Chocolate and other food preparations containing cocoa: bars, filled chocolates, chocolate candy, bulk chocolate, chocolate crumb, coatings and sweetened cocoa powder. Retail bars pay 5.6% or 6%; bulk and sweetened products are under tariff-rate quotas, with over-quota rates up to 52.8¢/kg + 8.5%. The only heading that pays the 2026 Section 301 duties.

workedExamples.title: $20,000 of chocolate bars from Belgium
workedExamples.body: Unfilled bars pay a 6% base rate. seo.title: HTS Chapter 18 Cocoa & Chocolate Tariff Updates 2026 — What Changed Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 18 (cocoa and chocolate) since January 2025: cocoa exempted from the reciprocal tariff, the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, and the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on chocolate by country, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 18 general rate changed between them. Sixteen statistical lines are new (organic cocoa beans, cocoa powder and chocolate are now reported separately, at the same rates), and on 19 over-quota chocolate lines the last staged Colombia and Panama FTA rates were removed.

The extra duties are what moved. The 2025 IEEPA tariffs hit cocoa until **November 13, 2025**, when cocoa beans, paste, butter and unsweetened powder (1801–1805) were exempted; chocolate kept paying until all IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**. The 10% Section 122 surcharge that followed also spared 1801–1805 and expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** a Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5% applies to products of 60 economies, but again **only to chocolate (1806)**: cocoa ingredients are on the exemption list. China pays 20% on chocolate (7.5% on cocoa, List 4A) and Brazil 37.5% on chocolate. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt.**

Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Cameroon, three of the largest cocoa suppliers, are not among the 60 economies. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 18 general-rate changes
changes.detail: All 91 Chapter 18 lines carry the same General and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. Sixteen statistical lines are new because organic cocoa beans (1801.00.00.10), cocoa powder (1805.00.00.10) and several chocolate lines are now reported separately, at the same rates. On 19 over-quota chocolate lines (for example 1806.20.26 and 1806.90.10) the remaining staged Colombia and Panama FTA rates, such as 2.4¢/kg + 0.2%, were removed from the special column.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S, S+) still apply to Canadian and Mexican chocolate.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs — cocoa exempt
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Cocoa beans, shells, paste, butter and unsweetened powder (1801–1805) were on the product exemption list (9903.03.03); chocolate (1806) paid it. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of cocoa and chocolate rose from **$8.25B in 2024 to $13.32B in 2025** (+61%). Almost all of the increase is in cocoa ingredients, and it is both price and volume. Cocoa beans rose from $1.13B to $2.82B: the quantity grew from 198,174 t to 322,247 t and the average value from $5.73 to $8.76 per kg (in 2023 it was $2.99). Cocoa butter rose from $1.09B to $2.25B, with 88,225 t becoming 117,015 t at $19.24 instead of $12.35 per kg. Chocolate (1806) grew more slowly, from $4.92B to $5.86B, on almost the same tonnage (757,316 t to 760,127 t).

The two halves of the chapter come from different places. **Beans, paste and butter come from the tropics**: Ecuador ($965M), Côte d'Ivoire ($728M) and Ghana ($439M) for beans, Côte d'Ivoire for paste, Indonesia and Malaysia for butter. **Chocolate comes from North America and Europe**: Canada alone shipped $3.07B, then Mexico ($683M), Belgium, Germany, Türkiye and Italy.

The tariff schedule explains little of the 2025 jump: cocoa ingredients were Free or nearly free all year, and cocoa was exempted from the reciprocal tariff on November 13, 2025. Duty matters for chocolate, where most volume comes from Canada and Mexico under USMCA. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
For cocoa the total rate depends on **what** you import as much as **where** it comes from. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, taken from the current tariff schedule.

**Cocoa beans, paste, butter and powder (1801–1805) pay no extra duty from any country except China** (7.5%), because they are on the Section 301 exemption list. **Chocolate (1806) is where countries differ**: USMCA-qualifying chocolate from Canada and Mexico enters free, the EU pays 10% and Switzerland 12.5% in place of the base rate, the UK, Ecuador, Malaysia and Indonesia add 10%, Peru 12.5%, China 20% and Brazil 37.5%. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana are not among the 60 Section 301 economies and can claim AGOA, so their chocolate pays the base rate or nothing.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-11, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; AGOA (D) for Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana; the Peru TPA (PE) for Peru. AGOA was reauthorized on February 3, 2026 through December 31, 2026 (P.L. 119-75; USTR). GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020 and is not applied. An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)).
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.

Quota lines: most chocolate products come in pairs, an in-quota line (Free to 10%) and an over-quota "Other" line (for example 37.2¢/kg + 4.3%). Which one applies depends on whether the quota in additional U.S. notes 1–3 to Chapter 18, notes 7–9 to Chapter 17 or note 10 to Chapter 4 is still open on the entry date; check CBP's quota status. Select a cell to see the lines.

Canada and Mexico on the 32 over-quota chocolate lines: the USMCA rate is set in Chapter 98 and shown as "See 9823… (quota)". Mexican goods are Free there without a limit (9823.08.01, 9823.10.01). Canadian goods are Free only up to 1,919 t in 2026 for dairy-containing chocolate (9823.08.02) and 9,600 t a year for sugar-containing products (9823.10.02); above that the over-quota rate applies, and the Section 301 relief covers only goods entered free (U.S. note 52(g)).

EU and Swiss floors: 10% (EU) or 12.5% (Switzerland) replaces the base rate when the base rate or its ad valorem equivalent is lower. For compound over-quota rates the equivalent depends on the shipment's value per kg; the cells use $10 per kg, so cheaper chocolate can end up paying the over-quota rate instead.

Over-quota sugar and dairy chocolate lines can also owe a special agricultural safeguard duty (Chapter 99 subchapter IV, 9904.17 and 9904.18) during a quantity-based safeguard period announced by the Secretary of Agriculture, or based on the entry's value; it is not applied here.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 18: Cocoa and Cocoa Preparations — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Cocoa & Chocolate: FDA Rules, Quotas & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 18) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The FDA, CBP and quota rules for each HTS Chapter 18 line — prior notice, food facility registration, FSVP, chocolate standards of identity, sugar and dairy tariff-rate quotas — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, in-quota entry, AGOA, drawback.
keywords: import chocolate into the us requirements

tariffEngineering.intro:
Cocoa and chocolate are food, so every shipment goes through FDA: **prior notice before arrival, a registered foreign facility and an importer with a Foreign Supplier Verification Program**. Chocolate sold as "milk chocolate" or "white chocolate" must also meet the FDA standard of identity for that name.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** or **AGOA**, enter **bulk chocolate and sweetened cocoa inside its quota** rather than at the over-quota rate, or import **cocoa ingredients**, which are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties, and make the chocolate yourself. Each one depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on chocolate from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty plus the base rate: 6% + 10% on unfilled bars, or an over-quota rate such as 37.2¢/kg + 4.3% (Mexico, and Canada within its quotas)
levers.appliesTo: Chocolate (1806) and the dutiable cocoa lines, for goods that originate under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, on the invoice or any other document. The origin rule for heading 1806 is a change of heading or subheading: chocolate made in Canada or Mexico from imported cocoa paste, butter or powder can qualify (sweetened cocoa powder of 1806.10 has a 35% limit on non-originating sugar and cocoa powder). Cocoa paste, butter and powder (1801–1805) qualify only when made from inputs of another chapter, so pressing imported beans in Canada does not make the butter originating.
levers.caveat: On the 32 over-quota chocolate lines Canada's duty-free access is capped (9823.08.02: 1,919 t in 2026; 9823.10.02: 9,600 t a year, with a Canadian export certificate when USTR requires one); Mexico's is not. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin, Chapter 18)
HTSUS Ch. 98, subch. XXIII, U.S. notes 8 and 10
USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Enter bulk chocolate, crumb and sweetened cocoa inside the quota
levers.saves: The over-quota rate: for example 5% instead of 37.2¢/kg + 4.3% on chocolate over 5.5% butterfat, or 10% instead of 33.6¢/kg on sweetened cocoa powder
levers.appliesTo: The in-quota lines of 1806 ("Described in additional U.S. note …") and their over-quota "Other" counterparts
levers.document: Entry under the in-quota statistical number while the quota is open; CBP reports the fill status. For the sugar-containing products quota of additional U.S. note 8 to Chapter 17, an export certificate from the exporting country is required when that country uses them (15 CFR part 2015).
levers.caveat: Quotas fill during the year and some are tiny: 2,313 t a year for sweetened cocoa powder, 2,122,834 kg for low-butterfat chocolate and crumb, none at all under notes 7 and 9 to Chapter 17. Products of Mexico are excluded from the Chapter 18 quotas (they use USMCA instead). The Section 301 duty for the country applies either way.

levers.title: Claim AGOA on cocoa products and chocolate from sub-Saharan Africa
levers.saves: The base rate: 0.2¢/kg on defatted paste, 0.52¢/kg on cocoa powder, 5.6% or 6% on chocolate bars
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose special column lists D, for goods of the countries in General Note 16 (including Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Nigeria)
levers.document: Evidence that the goods are the growth, product or manufacture of a beneficiary country and meet the 35% value-content rule, imported directly.
levers.caveat: AGOA runs through December 31, 2026 (P.L. 119-75). It does not cover the over-quota chocolate lines, and it does not lift a Section 301 duty: Nigeria, unlike Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, is one of the 60 economies (+12.5% on chocolate).

citations.label: USTR statement on the AGOA reauthorization (February 3, 2026)

levers.title: Claim another FTA (Peru, Colombia, Korea, Singapore and others)
levers.saves: The base rate on most non-quota lines; on 19 over-quota lines the last staged Colombia and Panama rates have been removed
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose special column lists the agreement's code
levers.document: The origin certification or documentation the agreement requires (19 CFR part 10 and the agreement's General Note).
levers.caveat: An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)): Peruvian chocolate still pays 12.5%. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Import cocoa ingredients, not finished chocolate
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty (10%–12.5%, 37.5% for Brazil) and the chocolate base rate
levers.appliesTo: Businesses that can make chocolate in the U.S. from beans, paste, butter or powder (1801–1805)
levers.document: Ordinary entry under the 1801–1805 line; the exemption in U.S. note 52(b) applies automatically to those headings.
levers.caveat: China still pays 7.5% (List 4A) on cocoa ingredients. Chocolate made in the U.S. must meet the same FDA standards of identity as imported chocolate.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86)

levers.title: Buy bulk chocolate in blocks of 4.5 kg or more
levers.saves: The base rate: blocks or slabs of 4.5 kg or more each (1806.20.20) are Free, against 4.3%–8.5% or a quota rate for other bulk chocolate
levers.appliesTo: Bulk chocolate of 1806.20 bought by confectioners and bakers
levers.document: Commercial invoice and packing list showing the block weight; a ruling if the classification is unclear.
levers.caveat: The Section 301 duty for the country still applies (EU 10%, Canada 10% unless USMCA). Classification follows the goods as imported, not how they are labeled.

levers.title: Claim drawback on chocolate you export again
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duty paid on imported goods that are exported or used to make exported goods
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable chocolate and cocoa products that leave the United States
levers.document: A drawback claim filed with CBP within 5 years of import, with proof of export and, for manufacturing drawback, a ruling or privilege.
levers.caveat: Check with CBP whether each Chapter 99 duty on your entry is eligible. Records of import, use and export must be kept.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: the sugar, butterfat and milk-solids content decides which quota line, and which rate, applies
levers.appliesTo: Any 1806 product where the composition or form decides the line
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its composition and its packaging.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the product described; a new recipe may need its own.

rules.title: Prior notice of imported food: submitted and confirmed before arrival (2 hours by road, 4 by rail or air, 8 by water)
Food facility registration: the foreign facility that manufactures, processes, packs or holds the food must be registered with FDA
Foreign Supplier Verification Program: the U.S. importer must verify that each foreign supplier meets U.S. food-safety standards

Standards of identity for cacao products: a product sold as cocoa, chocolate liquor, sweet, milk or white chocolate must meet the composition rules (e.g. milk chocolate ≥ 10% chocolate liquor and ≥ 12% milk solids)
Food labeling for packaged products: statement of identity, ingredient list and nutrition facts
Country-of-origin marking on the goods or their container

Tariff-rate quota lines: in-quota entry only while the quota is open (check CBP fill status); export certificates for the sugar-containing products quota where required; possible agricultural safeguard duty on over-quota lines

groups.label: Cocoa beans, whole or broken, raw or roasted
groups.note: Raw beans are a food under FDA rules even though they will be processed: prior notice, a registered facility and FSVP apply. Free for every country; only China pays an extra 7.5%.

groups.label: Cocoa shells, husks, skins and other cocoa waste
groups.note: Shells and husks imported for food or feed use follow the same FDA rules. Free, and no extra duty except China (7.5%).

groups.label: Cocoa paste, whether or not defatted
groups.note: Chocolate liquor sold as such must meet 21 CFR 163.111 (50%–60% cacao fat).

groups.label: Cocoa butter, fat and oil
groups.note: Cocoa butter is an ingredient; the standards of identity in 21 CFR part 163 govern the chocolate it goes into, not the butter itself.

groups.label: Cocoa powder, not containing added sugar or other…
groups.note: Cocoa sold as "cocoa", "breakfast cocoa" or "lowfat cocoa" must meet 21 CFR 163.112–163.114.

groups.label: Chocolate and other food preparations containing cocoa
groups.note: Most products come in quota pairs: the in-quota line (Free to 10%) and the over-quota "Other" line (up to 52.8¢/kg + 8.5%). Sugar content, butterfat content, milk solids and whether the product is for retail sale decide the line.

seo.title: Cocoa & Chocolate Tariffs FAQ: Cocoa Beans, Canada, Belgian & Swiss Chocolate, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 18) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about cocoa and chocolate tariffs: is there a tariff on cocoa beans or cocoa powder, chocolate from Canada, Belgium and Switzerland, the 2025 cocoa tariff exemption, HS codes for cocoa and chocolate, and where U.S. cocoa comes from.
keywords: is there a tariff on cocoa beans
is there a tariff on cocoa powder

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing cocoa and chocolate into the U.S. — tariffs by product and country, HS codes and where the trade comes from. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Cocoa beans, paste, butter and unsweetened powder (1801–1805) are Free or nearly free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties; only China pays an extra 7.5%.

Chocolate (1806) pays a base rate (6% on most bars) and, since July 24, 2026, a Section 301 duty for 60 economies: 10% in total for the EU, 12.5% for Switzerland, +10% for the UK, +20% for China, +37.5% for Brazil.

USMCA-qualifying chocolate from Canada and Mexico enters free, but Canada's free access on bulk chocolate and sweetened products is capped by quota. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana pay no extra duty and can claim AGOA through December 31, 2026.
The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026; cocoa had already been exempted on November 13, 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on cocoa beans?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on cocoa beans
are there tariffs on cocoa beans
faqs.answer: No, for almost every country. Cocoa beans (1801.00) have a Free base rate and are on the exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86) and the Brazil tariff, so Ecuador, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and every other supplier pay $0. Only beans from China pay 7.5% (Section 301 List 4A). The U.S. imported $2.82B of cocoa beans in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on cocoa powder?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on cocoa powder
faqs.answer: Unsweetened cocoa powder (1805.00) pays 0.52¢/kg, which is Free with most FTA claims and AGOA, and it is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. Sweetened cocoa powder is chocolate (1806.10): inside its quotas it pays Free or 10%, above them 21.7¢/kg or 33.6¢/kg, plus any Section 301 duty for the country.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on chocolate from Canada?
faqs.answer: Not on USMCA-qualifying chocolate: it enters free and is exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian goods (9903.05.93). On bulk dairy and sugar chocolate lines, Canada's free access is capped by USMCA quotas (1,919 t in 2026 and 9,600 t a year). Chocolate that doesn't qualify pays its base rate plus 10%, for example 6% + 10% = 16% on unfilled bars. The 35% IEEPA duty ended on February 24, 2026. Canada shipped $3.07B of chocolate to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there an import duty on cocoa and chocolate from Mexico?
faqs.answer: USMCA-qualifying cocoa products and chocolate from Mexico enter free on every line, with no quota limit on the bulk chocolate lines (9823.08.01, 9823.10.01) and no Section 301 duty (9903.05.94). Goods that don't qualify pay the base rate, plus 10% on chocolate. Chocolate made in Mexico from imported cocoa paste or butter can qualify; cocoa butter pressed in Mexico from imported beans cannot. Mexico shipped $683M of chocolate in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Belgian or European chocolate?
faqs.answer: 10% of value since July 24, 2026. For EU products whose base rate is under 10%, the Section 301 action charges 10% in place of the base rate (9903.05.39), and chocolate bars are 5.6% or 6% at base. A $20,000 pallet of Belgian bars pays $2,000. The 15% reciprocal rate of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Swiss chocolate?
faqs.answer: 12.5% of value for chocolate made in Switzerland: the Section 301 action charges 12.5% in place of the base rate when the base rate is lower (9903.05.74), and the Swiss exception list names no chocolate. The rate follows the country where the chocolate was made, not the brand. The 39% IEEPA rate of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Did Trump exempt cocoa from tariffs?
faqs.answer: Yes, cocoa but not chocolate. Executive Order 14360 exempted cocoa beans, shells, paste, butter and unsweetened powder from the reciprocal tariffs from November 13, 2025; chocolate kept paying until all IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. The same cocoa lines were exempt from the 2026 Section 122 surcharge and are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties, which do apply to chocolate.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for cocoa beans, cocoa powder and cocoa butter?
faqs.answer: Cocoa beans, whole or broken (which includes cocoa nibs), are 1801.00; shells and husks 1802.00; cocoa paste or mass 1803 (1803.10 not defatted, 1803.20 defatted); cocoa butter 1804.00; cocoa powder without added sugar 1805.00. Sweetened cocoa powder is 1806.10. Organic beans and powder have their own 10-digit lines (1801.00.00.10, 1805.00.00.10).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for chocolate?
faqs.answer: Heading 1806. Chocolate bars and blocks are 1806.31 if filled (5.6%) and 1806.32 if not filled (most at 6%); chocolate candy and other preparations not in bars are 1806.90 (mostly 6%); bulk chocolate over 2 kg is 1806.20 (Free in blocks of 4.5 kg or more); sweetened cocoa powder is 1806.10. Products with more sugar, butterfat or milk solids fall on quota lines.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. get its cocoa and chocolate from?
searchedAs: where does the us get cocoa beans from
where does the us get most of its cocoa
where does the us get most of its chocolate
faqs.answer: Cocoa beans mostly come from Ecuador ($965M in 2025), Côte d'Ivoire ($728M) and Ghana ($439M); cocoa butter from Indonesia and Malaysia; cocoa powder from the Netherlands. Chocolate mostly comes from Canada ($3.07B) and Mexico ($683M), then Belgium and Germany. In total the U.S. imported $13.32B of Chapter 18 goods in 2025, up from $8.25B in 2024.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on cocoa and chocolate from Côte d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast)?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on cocoa
faqs.answer: Côte d'Ivoire is not one of the 60 economies in the 2026 Section 301 action, so it pays only base rates: Free on beans, paste and butter, and Free under AGOA on cocoa powder and most non-quota chocolate lines (AGOA runs through December 31, 2026). The 15% IEEPA reciprocal duty ended on February 24, 2026; cocoa had been exempt from it since November 13, 2025.
